records.name_note: Only one admissible source has a dedicated page for this exact species (NC State); RHS lists only cultivar pages and MoBot could not be read. NC State's Common Name(s) list shows Giant Bamburanta first and Never Never Plant second, and the Description opens with "The Giant Bamburanta" and then says "Another common name for this plant is the Never Never Plant", so Giant Bamburanta is used as common_name and Never Never Plant is the alternate. NC State lists the former names Calathea oppenheimiana, Maranta herderiana, Maranta oppenheimiana and Phyllodes oppenheimiana. The "Tricolor" cultivar is kept out of species-level fields.
unknowns: Pet toxicity: the NC State page for this species has no toxicity block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags; no admissible source addressed it, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null (not 'safe').
Edibility: no admissible source addresses eating this plant; is_edible is null.

Only NC State has a dedicated page for this exact species. RHS lists only cultivar pages (e.g. 'Tricolor', 'Variegata', 'Amagris'), which are not used. The MoBot plantfinder host failed TLS verification from this environment, so no MoBot page was read. Clemson, UF/IFAS, PSU, UMD and UGA yielded no page for this species.

chill_damage_f is null. NC State's only temperature figure is its Intolerant line, 'Intolerant: direct sunlight; temperatures less than 60 degrees F.; cold drafts; cold or hard water; constantly dry air; direct fertilization after repotting;'. That is an intolerance statement, not a stated damage-onset temperature, and this catalog's landing rules do not admit an intolerance threshold as a damage onset, so the research value of 60 was not landed. The USDA zone list (10b-12b) is a hardiness rating and was not used either.

water_regime is null: NC State gives 'moist and well-drained soil' (a soil adjective) and under/overwatering symptoms, but no watering instruction. Watering intervals, dry-down target and check depth are null.
soil_drainage is moderate from 'moist and well-drained soil' and the bare Good Drainage + Moist tag pair. No source states consistently moist soil as a requirement, so moisture_retentive is not set.

Fertilizing: NC State says only 'fertilized monthly during its growth cycle'. That is a word-based cadence with no stated day count, no active months and no dilution strength, so all three fields are null.

Soil pH: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) together, and the open-ended bands give no usable floor or ceiling, so both pH fields are null. soil_base is null because no source names a potting mix.

direct_sun_hours_max is null: the '2-6 hours' sits in the Partial Shade light-category label (site-wide legend), and the species prose says bright indirect sun and intolerance of direct sunlight, with no hour figure. light_fc fields are null. outdoor_sun_exposure part_shade comes from the structured Light field, although the plant is chiefly a houseplant (NC State zones 10b-12b).

Temperature ranges: NC State gives no day or night range, only the 60 F intolerance line and 'Drafts should be avoided' (its Intolerant list also names 'cold drafts'), so day/night fields are null. humidity_pct is null because only 'high to medium humidity' and a '#high humidity' tag are given; humidity_need is high but the prose says 'high to medium'.
Pollinators: flowers are described as inconspicuous and there is no Attracts field, so attracts_pollinators is null.

Mature size is NC State's Dimensions block (Height 1 ft. 8 in. - 3 ft. 3 in., Width the same), converted to inches (20-39); the prose also says it grows up to 3 feet tall and may take 5-10 years to reach ultimate height. These figures are not cultivar-specific.

records.name_note: Only NC State has a dedicated page for this exact name among the admissible sources I could locate. Its rendered Common Name(s) list reads Friendship Plant then Panamiga (the list is alphabetized), and its Description opens with 'The Friendship Plant'. Friendship Plant is used as the common name. NC State lists the former names Pilea pubescens var. involucrata and Urtica involucrata. NC State lists four cultivars ('Liner', 'Moon Valley', 'Norfolk', 'Silver'), so cultivar-specific content is excluded here. No content from Pilea peperomioides (Chinese Money Plant) or Pilea cadierei (Aluminum Plant) was used.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's dedicated Pilea involucrata page has no Poison block and gives no severity rating or poison-part list. Its tag list carries the separate tags "#non-toxic for cats", "#non-toxic for horses" and "#non-toxic for dogs", plus "#pet friendly", among twelve tags (the others are #houseplant, #showy leaves, #colorful, #terrarium, #easy to propagate, #interesting leaves, #easy to grow and #container plant). These are tags only, with no symptom or handling text. No other admissible source was found to confirm or contradict them.
unknowns: Only NC State has a dedicated page for Pilea involucrata among the admissible sources I could locate. I found no dedicated page at RHS (its site search returned only Salvia involucrata), and I found no Missouri Botanical Garden, UF/IFAS or Clemson page. The plantfinder.mobot.org and ask.ifas.ufl.edu hosts were also not readable from the sandbox.

No numeric temperature range, chill-damage onset, humidity percentage or light level (footcandles) is given on the NC State page, so those fields are null. The page says only 'warm, humid environment in bright indirect light'.

water_regime is null. NC State says 'Water moderately in the growing season, less in fall to late winter', which does not map to a regime token, and it gives no dry-down target or day interval. Its Soil Drainage field values are Good Drainage and Moist, which fit the moderate drainage reading.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null. NC State's Acid (<6.0) band is open-ended, and the Neutral (6.0-8.0) band's closed top could not be checked against an RHS pH field because no RHS page exists for this species.

direct_sun_hours_max is null. The only hour figure is the generic '2-6 hours' inside NC State's Partial Shade light-category label, which is site-wide legend text, not species-specific prose. outdoor_sun_exposure part_shade comes from NC State's Light field values Dappled Sunlight and Partial Shade. The page lists USDA zone 11a-12b and recommends growing it indoors in bright indirect light; this is mainly an indoor plant.
Fertilizer guidance is not given on the NC State page, so the fertilize fields are null.

is_edible and attracts_pollinators are null because the page does not address either. The pet-safety tags are the only toxicity evidence, and they are unscoped beyond cats, dogs and horses. The page has no human-toxicity Poison block.
mature_height_in and mature_spread_in come from NC State's Dimensions block, which gives Height and Width as 0 ft. 3 in. to 1 ft. 0 in. That converts to 3-12 inches for each.

records.name_note: Sources split on the primary common name; the entry was requested as Strawberry Begonia. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list (alphabetized; the page-title parenthetical shows the same order) gives Creeping Saxifrage, Strawberry Begonia, Strawberry Geranium, Strawberry Saxifrage, while NC State's description prose opens with Strawberry Begonia, 'also called "Mother of Thousands"'. RHS's dedicated page renders the subtitle creeping saxifrage and lists strawberry begonia, strawberry geranium and strawberry saxifrage among nine names in its Other common names field (which also includes mother of thousands). Creeping Saxifrage was chosen because it is the first common name on both dedicated pages: the first item of NC State's Common Name(s) list and title parenthetical, and the RHS Plant Profile subtitle. Mother of Thousands is already this catalog's landed name for Kalanchoe daigremontiana, so it is not used here.
unknowns: MoBot Plant Finder page for Saxifraga stolonifera (kempercode=c251) could not be loaded in this session (TLS certificate verification failure on plantfinder.mobot.org), so no MoBot content is used or cited.
toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: the NC State page for this exact name has no toxicity block and no admissible source reached for this exact name states pet safety or toxicity.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm and the day-interval fields left null: NC State's 'moist, organically rich, well-drained soils' is a soil description, not a watering statement, and no reached admissible source gives a watering instruction for this species. Soil_drainage moderate rests on NC State's Good Drainage and Moist tags plus the moist-but-well-drained prose; its Occasionally Wet tag is also present and does not change the reading.
soil_base left null: no reached source names a potting mix for indoor culture or says in-ground bed soil for the groundcover use; indoor and outdoor are not merged.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0) all together, which are open-ended bands, and RHS lists acid or alkaline or neutral soils as acceptable.

Indoor light: NC State says indoors it should be sited in bright indirect light, with some non-intense direct sun promoting reddish leaf color, but gives no foot-candle or hour figure, so light_fc_min, light_fc_good and direct_sun_hours_max are null. The generic hour ranges in NC State's light legend were not used.
outdoor_sun_exposure is shade-only (part_shade, full_shade) from NC State's Light tags and prose and RHS's Position (Full shade, Partial shade); no source reached supports sun values.

chill_damage_f null: NC State gives USDA hardiness (prose Zones 6 through 9; structured field 6a-10b) and RHS gives UK hardiness rating H2, which are survival ratings, not damage-onset temperatures. Temperature, humidity, fertilizer, pH, edibility and pollinator fields have no admissible-source statement and are null.

Size is NC State's Dimensions block (0 ft 6 in to 1 ft 6 in tall, 1 ft 0 in to 2 ft 0 in wide). RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread of 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 inches) for its own plant profile, which broadly agrees; NC State was used as the anchor.

The RHS page for this taxon is titled Saxifraga stolonifera (5); RHS lists synonyms Saxifraga ligulata and Saxifraga sarmentosa. NC State's Plant Type field carries three values (Ground Cover, Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial); NC State's leaf characteristic is Semi-evergreen while its description says evergreen.

RHS's Name Status row for Saxifraga stolonifera reads Correct; it is not cited because the bare one-word value cannot locate its field and the label+value pair is a concatenation. scientific_name_accepted rests on NC State's H1 and RHS's rendered H1.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated Dracaena surculosa page gives five common names alphabetically, in both its page-title parenthetical and its rendered Common Name(s) list: Dracena, Florida Beauty, Gold Dust, Gold Dust Dracaena, Spotted Dracaena. The first item, 'Dracena', is a misspelling of the genus name and so is an umbrella term, not this species' name. The Description prose opens with 'Gold dust dracena', and the page later spells the same name 'Gold dust dracaena' ('Gold dust dracaena can be grown outdoors in a container on a patio in the summer'), so Gold Dust Dracaena is landed. NC State gives the former names as Draco surculosa and Pleomele surculosa.
records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Plant Toolbox, Dracaena surculosa. Under the page's 'Poisonous to Humans:' heading the Poison block reads: Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: "Toxic to humans, cats, and dogs if ingested. Vomiting (occasionally with blood), depression, anorexia, hypersalivation, dilated pupils (cats)" (the dilated pupils entry is scoped to cats specifically); Poison Toxic Principle: Saponins; Causes Contact Dermatitis: No; Poison Part: Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. The severity rating sits under the human-scoped heading; the symptom line itself names humans, cats and dogs. The Problems field separately lists 'Poisonous to Humans', 'Problem for Cats' and 'Problem for Dogs', and the page-top banner reads 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.' Plant Type values co-listed: Herbaceous Perennial, Houseplant, Perennial, Poisonous, Shrub. The tag list includes #poisonous, #problem for dogs, #problem for cats and #poisonous if ingested. No separate handling warning is stated, and no second admissible source was found to confirm or contradict it.
unknowns: Only NC State has a dedicated page for Dracaena surculosa among the admissible sources I could read; RHS returned 404 for dracaena-surculosa, Clemson returned 403, and no dedicated MoBot, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD or UGA page was located. Fields needing a second source (fertilizing, pH, soil mix, light intensity, pollinators) are null.
soil_base is null: NC State gives no potting mix. soil_ph_min/max null: no pH stated.

water_regime keep_moist rests on NC State's 'Keep the soil moist during the regular growing season, but overwatering and standing water will cause root rot'; the root-rot caveat means this is moist, not wet, and no dry-down target or interval is given, so water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm and the day estimates are null.

night_f_min 50 comes from NC State's advice to bring the container plant inside below 50 F at night; it is a bring-in threshold, not a stated damage onset, so chill_damage_f and cool_rest_note are null.
direct_sun_hours_max is null: NC State says 'bright but not direct light' with no hours figure. light_fc_min/light_fc_good null: no foot-candle figures.

outdoor_sun_exposure comes from NC State's structured Light field (Dappled Sunlight -> part_shade; Deep shade -> full_shade); this is chiefly a houseplant and the Light field is the only structured sun statement.

Toxicity: the Low severity rating is human-scoped (Poisonous to Humans block); the cat and dog statement is in the same block's Poison Symptoms plus separate Problem for Cats / Problem for Dogs tags. No second admissible source was found, so no disagreement on scope can be checked.
is_edible false is based on the 'Toxic to humans ... if ingested' symptom line; no source describes any use as food.
attracts_pollinators null: NC State has no Attracts field and the flower description (fragrant at night) does not name pollinators.
Name trap: Aucuba japonica is also called gold dust plant and is a different, landed species; nothing here was borrowed from it or from the other landed Dracaena records.

records.name_note: The sources split on the primary name. RHS's rendered plant-profile subtitle and MoBot's prose both lead with 'white evening primrose', and RHS lists 'Mexican evening primrose, pink ladies' as other common names. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list gives, in alphabetical order, Mexican Evening Primrose, Pink Buttercups, Pink Evening Primrose, Pink Ladies, Showy Evening Primrose, and NC State's Description prose opens with 'Showy Evening Primrose'. Two of the three dedicated pages lead with white evening primrose, so that is used as common_name; Showy Evening Primrose is NC State's lead. 'Pink Evening Primrose' is a name given by NC State and by MoBot's additional-common-names sentence, not the lead name of any dedicated page. NC State lists Hartmannia speciosa and Oenothera berlandieri as previous names.
records.toxicity_detail: No admissible source gives a poison-part list, symptom list or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag for this species. The NC State page carries no Poison block. NC State's Edibility field reads: 'Cook as greens or in salads, best flavor when collected before flowering'. NC State also tags the plant #edible and lists Edible among its Plant Type values, but it does not name which plant part is the edible one.
unknowns: is_houseplant is false: NC State's Landscape Location field lists Meadow, Naturalized Area and Slope/Bank and its hardiness field gives zones 5a-8b; no admissible source addresses indoor culture.
toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible source gives any toxicity information for cats or dogs, and the NC State page has no Poison block or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags.

Edibility is conditional: NC State's Edibility field says 'Cook as greens or in salads, best flavor when collected before flowering'. NC State does not name the plant part and gives no toxicity data. MoBot and RHS do not address eating. Only NC State addresses edibility, so there is no disagreement between sources, but it is a single-source claim.

Common name: RHS (rendered subtitle) and MoBot (prose 'commonly called white evening primrose') lead with 'white evening primrose'; NC State's Description prose opens with 'Showy Evening Primrose', and its alphabetized Common Name(s) list includes Pink Evening Primrose. MoBot's prose also gives pink evening primrose, pink ladies and showy evening primrose as additional common names.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's Light field lists both Full sun and Partial Shade (2-6 hours), but MoBot's Sun field (Full sun) and RHS's Position (Full sun) list only full sun. part_shade is therefore left out. MoBot's 'tolerates some afternoon part shade' is a tolerance aside. NC State's Description says it grows in shade as a groundcover but does not flower there.

soil_drainage: NC State's Soil Drainage field values Good Drainage, Moist and Occasionally Dry map to moderate. MoBot says well-drained soils with good drainage, and RHS's structured Moisture field reads Well–drained. RHS's Cultivation paragraph looks like genus-level text and is not used as species evidence. No source describes a sharp or sandy drainage requirement with no tolerance for wet soil, so fast was not set. NC State's Description says it grows in any soil types except poor drainage ones.

water_regime is null. The audit read MoBot's structured Water field as 'Dry to medium' (a value that would map to dry_surface_between), but Missouri Botanical Garden refuses this machine's non-browser clients, so the field cannot be quote-checked and is not cited. MoBot's Culture sentence ('average, dry to medium moisture, well-drained soils') is a soil description, not a watering statement. NC State and RHS give no watering instruction; NC State says only 'It will go dormant if it receives no moisture in summer.' Drought tolerance was not used to set a regime.

soil_ph: NC State lists Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), which are open-ended or partial bands. RHS lists acid, alkaline or neutral. No floor or ceiling can be set from them, so both are left null.

Temperature, humidity, light-fc, fertilizer and watering-interval fields are left null: no admissible source states them. NC State zones 5a-8b, MoBot zone 4 to 9 and RHS H5 are hardiness ratings, not chill-damage onset temperatures.

Mature size: the NC State page has no Dimensions block, so the RHS 'Max Height' and 'Max Spread' fields were used (0.1-0.5 metres = 3.9-19.7 in, x39.37). RHS is UK-calibrated and takes 2-5 years to reach maturity. MoBot gives larger US figures, 10-24 inches tall (0.75 to 2.00 feet) and 18 inches wide or more (1.00 to 1.50 feet), so real-world size is likely larger than the RHS range.

NC State (spreads by stoloniferous rootstocks and seeds) and MoBot (spreads by rhizomes and self-seeding) describe spreading by rhizomes and by seed. RHS describes creeping rhizomes and a suckering habit. NC State says it can take over a perennial garden, MoBot says sometimes aggressively, and RHS says occasionally invasive.
NC State Plant Type lists three values: Edible, Ground Cover and Herbaceous Perennial. The 'Woody Plant Leaf Characteristics: Deciduous' entry is a separate field.
Not cited, so no contrast was recorded: no contrast with Oenothera lindheimeri or Oenothera fruticosa was made in name_note, since it would need citations to those species' own pages.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the accepted binomial and on the lead common name. NC State's dedicated page is headed Valeriana rubra and lists Centranthus ruber under 'Previously known as:'; RHS profiles the same plant under the heading Centranthus ruber, with red valerian as its common name and Jupiter's beard among its other common names. scientific_name_accepted follows NC State's current name, Valeriana rubra (the reclassification is followed and disclosed), and the RHS page is used as a same-taxon synonym page, not a dedicated page for the exact name. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list gives Jupiter's Beard, Keys of Heaven, Red-Spur, Red Valerian, Spur Valerian in alphabetical order, and its Description opens with 'Red valerian'. common_name is therefore Red Valerian, with Jupiter's Beard also listed by NC State.
records.toxicity_detail: No toxicity statement was found on the admissible pages. NC State's Valeriana rubra page carries an Edibility field and a Description passage, reproduced here: Edibility: 'The leaves and roots can be eaten.' Description: 'Its leaves and roots are both edible.  The leaves can be eaten raw or lightly boiled.  The roots can be used in preparing soups.' NC State's Plant Type field lists Edible, Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial; its Leaf Value To Gardener field lists Edible. The page has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tags. Do not borrow the medicinal or sedative content of true valerian (Valeriana officinalis).
unknowns: is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type field (Edible, Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial) and zones 5a-8b frame an outdoor perennial, and RHS suggests flower borders and beds; no source frames it as a houseplant. chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, temperature ranges, humidity, indoor light and direct_sun_hours_max left null: no admissible source addresses them for this plant (NC State's 'does not grow well in hot humid climates' is a climate remark, not a humidity need).

toxic_to_pets and toxicity: NC State's Valeriana rubra page has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags, and no other admissible source consulted states toxicity; recorded as no record, not as safe. Edibility is NC State's: leaves and roots, unconditional on that page; no other source checked for edibility.

soil_drainage left null: NC State lists Soil Texture Sand, Soil Drainage Good Drainage and Occasionally Dry and warns 'Continuously wet soil can lead to crown rot', and RHS says well-drained, ideally chalky or stony, but no source states sharp drainage, so fast was not set; the Good Drainage + Occasionally Dry pair is also not the Good Drainage + Moist pair that maps to moderate.

water_regime and all watering/fertilizer fields left null: no admissible source read states a watering or feeding statement. A Missouri Botanical Garden page for Centranthus ruber could not be fetched (connection error), so it was not consulted.

soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Alkaline (>8.0), an open-ended band, and RHS lists pH 'Alkaline or Neutral'. soil_ph_min 6.0 is the lower edge of NC State's closed Neutral (6.0-8.0) band; NC State lists no Acid band for this plant.

outdoor_sun_exposure: full_sun only. NC State's Light field also lists Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours), but RHS's structured Position lists Full sun only and RHS Cultivation says Needs full sun to flower well, so part_shade was dropped.

Size is NC State's Dimensions block (2-4 ft tall, 1-2 ft wide, converted to inches). RHS Max Height 0.5-1 metres and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (about 20-39 in and 4-20 in) differ from NC State in both height and spread and were not used; no cultivar sizes used.
NC State flags this plant as weedy with invasive tendencies and high invasive potential in some counties; relevant to recommending it for planting.

Taxonomy: NC State accepts Valeriana rubra (previously Centranthus ruber); RHS marks Centranthus ruber as Correct. The RHS page is a synonym-name page for the same plant, used only for the name split, pH and the soil_base wording.

RHS's Name Status row for its Centranthus ruber page reads Correct, so RHS and NC State disagree on the genus; the bare one-word value is not cited (it cannot locate its field, and the label+value pair is a concatenation).

records.name_note: The expected name 'Heartleaf Bergenia' appears on neither admissible page; NC State's page for Bergenia crassifolia lists Bergenia cordifolia under 'Previously known as:'. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list is alphabetized and leads with the bare genus word 'Bergenia' (Leather Bergenia is second, followed by Pigsqueak, Siberian Tea and Winter blooming bergenia), and its Description prose also opens with 'Bergenia', so NC State offers no species-specific lead name. RHS's dedicated page renders the subtitle Korean elephant's ears beneath the heading Bergenia crassifolia and lists 'elephant ears, elephant's ear saxifrage' as other common names, so RHS's subtitle Korean elephant's ears is used as common_name. Leather Bergenia, the research record's name, is only NC State's second list entry, not a lead name.
unknowns: Edibility (NC State, Edibility field): 'The leaves are used as a tea substitute.' NC State's description adds that the leaves give the common name Siberian Tea and that roots, leaves and stems contain tannin. No preparation times or conditions are stated. is_edible is true for the leaves only; no source addresses other parts.
Toxicity: neither admissible page fetched (NC State, RHS) states any toxicity, so toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail are null. NC State's page carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags.

The Missouri Botanical Garden / plantfinder.mobot.org page could not be loaded (connection failed on repeated tries), and Clemson HGIC returned 403; no other admissible page for this exact taxon was found, so those sources are not used. No UF/IFAS, PSU, UMD or UGA page was located.

The expected name 'Heartleaf Bergenia' is not on the NC State or RHS page for B. crassifolia. NC State's list and its Description prose both lead with the bare genus word 'Bergenia'; RHS leads with 'Korean elephant's ears' and lists 'elephant ears, elephant's ear saxifrage' as other common names and Bergenia coreana as synonym (not cordifolia). NC State's first item is a bare genus word and RHS's lead, Korean elephant's ears, is the usable lead name, so common_name is Korean Elephant's Ears. RHS's Name Status row reads Correct (not cited as a bare value).

mature size: NC State gives Height 1 ft 0 in - 1 ft 6 in and Width 0 ft 9 in - 2 ft 0 in (12-18 in and 9-24 in, used). RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in) and describes 'to 50cm high and wide', which is broader; NC State's own-page block is the anchor.
Soil pH: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) and RHS lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', so soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null (open-ended bands).

water_regime is null: NC State says it grows best in moist organic soil (a soil adjective) and that leaves dry out if soil stays dry for an extended period, and RHS says it 'dislikes extremes of heat and drought', but neither gives a watering instruction. This is an in-ground perennial, so dry-down and day-interval fields are null.
chill_damage_f is null: NC State says it 'will sustain winter damage in northern areas' and lists zones 3a-8b, and RHS rates H7; these are hardiness ratings, not damage-onset temperatures.
direct_sun_hours_max is null: only the site-wide light legend gives hours.
NC State has no Attracts field (only 'Play Value: Attractive Flowers'); RHS tags this plant 'Plants for pollinators', so attracts_pollinators is true on RHS's evidence.

is_houseplant is false: NC State's Landscape Location field lists Coastal, Rock Wall, Slope/Bank, Walkways and Woodland and its hardiness field gives zones 3a-8b; no source frames it as a houseplant. Humidity, indoor light, temperature and fertilizer fields are null: no admissible source addresses them.
RHS gives Position as Full shade, Full sun, Partial shade, consistent with the NC State-derived exposure values.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page is headed Phedimus kamtschaticus and lists the former names Phedimus floriferus, Sedum floriferum and Sedum kamtschaticum under 'Previously known as:'. RHS's dedicated profile is headed Sedum kamtschaticum, so RHS and NC State differ on the genus; scientific_name_accepted follows NC State's current name and the former name Sedum kamtschaticum is disclosed here. On the common name the sources split: NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Kamschatka Sedum, Orange Stonecrop, Stonecrop) and starts with Kamschatka Sedum, but NC State's Description opens with orange stonecrop and RHS's plant-profile subtitle gives orange stonecrop as its only common name, so Orange Stonecrop was chosen.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's 'Poisonous to Humans' block (human-scoped; this page carries no cat/dog tags): Poison Severity Low (the page also says 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.'); Poison Symptoms: Unknown, but possibly gastrointestinal symptoms; Poison Toxic Principle: Alkaloids sedine, sedamine and others; Causes Contact Dermatitis: No; Poison Part: Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. Plant Type tags on the page: Ground Cover, Poisonous. No admissible source scopes the risk to cats or dogs.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: NC State's poison data is human-scoped ('Poisonous to Humans') and no admissible source names cats or dogs.
RHS lists this species as Sedum kamtschaticum (Name Status Correct) while NC State uses Phedimus kamtschaticus; scientific_name_accepted follows NC State's dedicated page.

water_regime left null: NC State's Description gives 'dry to medium moisture' as a site preference and no admissible source states a watering instruction; the Missouri Botanical Garden page could not be fetched from this environment.
soil_drainage moderate rests on NC State's Good Drainage + Moist + Very Dry tags (spanning dry and moist) with a root-rot warning for poorly drained soils; not fast because Moist is also tagged.
soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Neutral band is (6.0-8.0) and RHS lists alkaline soils as acceptable.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's Light field gives only a minimum ('Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)') and no admissible source states a maximum.
is_edible left null: no admissible source addresses eating; NC State lists the plant as Poisonous with possible gastrointestinal symptoms and Low severity.

is_houseplant is false: NC State's Landscape Location field (Recreational Play Area), its zones 3a-9b and its rock-garden, ground-cover and edging uses frame an outdoor perennial; its container use is a patio container, not a houseplant framing. Temperature, humidity, light_fc, fertilizer and watering-interval fields left null: no admissible source states them. RHS's Max Height 'Up to 10 cm' has no lower bound and NC State's Dimensions were used instead.
Missouri Botanical Garden page (plantfinder.mobot.org) failed to load here, so it is not cited. The name 'Russian Stonecrop' is not supported by any fetched admissible source.

normalizations: 2026-10-09: b123 (mixed gaps: two houseplants, groundcovers and perennials) landed from the post-audit records. Eight species: Giant Bamburanta, Friendship Plant, Creeping Saxifrage, Gold Dust Dracaena, White Evening Primrose, Red Valerian, Korean Elephant's Ears, Orange Stonecrop. Auditor-supplied corrected wording used verbatim where it held; removed name_notes rebuilt on the journal's research text (wf_46607538-504) with only the audited sub-claims changed; every substitute quote ground-truthed with qc.py and a strict consecutive-node check (b123_qcheck.py) before it was applied. Landing decisions: Bergenia crassifolia lands as Korean Elephant's Ears, RHS's subtitle, because NC State's Common Name(s) list and Description prose both lead with the bare genus word 'Bergenia' (the research name Leather Bergenia is only NC State's second list entry; disclosed in name_note); Bergenia's attracts_pollinators restored true on RHS's 'Plants for pollinators' badge, as the audit confirmed; Red Valerian's outdoor_sun_exposure cut to full_sun (RHS Position Full sun only and 'Needs full sun to flower well.'); Giant Bamburanta's chill_damage_f 60 nulled (NC State's 'Intolerant: ... temperatures less than 60 degrees F.' is an intolerance statement, not a stated damage onset); White Evening Primrose's water_regime nulled (its only citation was a MoBot soil sentence and the audit's MoBot Water-field substitute cannot be checked from this machine); is_houseplant set false (NC State Landscape Location / Plant Type / hardiness-zone citations) for the four landscape species where it was null. Reclassifications followed and disclosed in name_note: Valeriana rubra (RHS: Centranthus ruber) and Phedimus kamtschaticus (RHS: Sedum kamtschaticum). Every <title>-only NC State parenthetical and RHS pipe-joined <title> replaced by the rendered Common Name(s) list, rendered H1 or rendered subtitle; every bare RHS 'Correct' dropped (two belonged to synonym pages, where the CORR form would corroborate the wrong name), the status kept in unknowns; Friendship Plant's space-joined tag line split into single tags; Gold Dust Dracaena's truncated Problems slice, bare 'No' and bare 'Saponins' replaced by full field / contiguous label-value runs, and the full Poison block cited for it and Orange Stonecrop. toxic_to_pets true for Gold Dust Dracaena (NC State Poison Symptoms and Problems: Problem for Cats/Dogs); false for Friendship Plant (separate #non-toxic for cats / #non-toxic for dogs tags); the rest null. No common name collided with a landed species.
